description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Microsoft says China-aligned Storm-0940 took over ConnectWise Cloud Backup’s app identities and used them to sign in to customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants — several reached privileged access
items.content_text: Microsoft said on 21 October that it assesses a China-state aligned actor it tracks as Storm-0940 was behind the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply-chain compromise. The attacker gained control of the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications tied to ConnectWise Cloud Backup (formerly SkyKick) and used them to sign in to customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants as the application, so multi-factor authentication never applied. Microsoft counts sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 tenants; most failed, but several reached privileged cloud access, some in under three hours, followed by directory reconnaissance, new app credentials and role changes. Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an open-source penetration-testing framework that can use any AI model; Microsoft does not attribute the earlier ARTEX intrusions at Korean financial firms to Storm-0940 (see that card). ConnectWise took the affected services offline, began a phased restoration on 21 October and says it has no evidence partner backup data was compromised. This leads because one vendor’s app identities opened a path into many organisations’ cloud tenants at once.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Threat Intelligence; ConnectWise via CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive; Huntress via BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Password spray 10–14 Oct 2026 (unsuccessful); phased restoration from 21 Oct 2026; Microsoft attribution 21 Oct 2026

items.title: Quest Diagnostics tells the SEC an intruder got into its Quanum lab-ordering system and likely viewed patient records — it says operations were not materially disrupted
items.content_text: In an 8-K filed on 22 October, Quest Diagnostics said it learned on 21 October of unauthorised access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, which some clients use to place test orders and look up results, and that it believes the intruder accessed certain patient records. It activated its incident-response procedures, notified federal law enforcement and brought in outside experts; the scope is still under investigation and no patient count has been given. Quest says the incident has not materially disrupted its business or its ability to serve patients, and it filed under Item 8.01 (other events) rather than the material-incident item. HIPAA Journal reports that access to the system was paused and that clients can still order and receive results by fax, paper, direct lab-system interfaces or electronic medical records. Quest told the Associated Press the breach is not related to the PHP2Shell flaws (see that card). No group has claimed it.

_threatfeed.source_name: Quest Diagnostics Form 8-K; Associated Press via SecurityWeek; HIPAA Journal
_threatfeed.date_note: Discovered 21 Oct 2026; 8-K filed 22 Oct 2026

items.title: Parkview Health took its Indiana–Ohio network offline after “suspicious activity” — MyChart is back with limits, but billing and video visits are still down
items.content_text: Parkview Health told patients on 18 October about a system-wide internet outage, and its 19 October update, as quoted by outlets, said it had proactively disabled its network in response to suspicious activity and had no indication that patient data was compromised. As of 23 October its website said Parkview MyChart and its Find a Doctor search had been restored with some limitations, with appointment reminders, messaging, refill requests and scheduling back, but billing and video visits still unavailable. Patients were told to call their provider’s office or use walk-in clinics, and to call 911 in an emergency. No electronic health record downtime or ambulance diversion has been reported, no ransomware group has claimed it and Parkview has not named a cause, so this is a suspected cyber incident rather than a confirmed attack.

_threatfeed.source_name: Parkview Health website; DailySecurityReview; HIPAA Journal
_threatfeed.date_note: Outage from 18 Oct 2026; network disabled per 19 Oct 2026 update; status 23 Oct 2026

items.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and Docker shipped a credential stealer and backdoor after attackers used maintainers’ stolen GitHub tokens to run the release
items.content_text: LiteLLM, a widely used open-source gateway that routes applications to AI model providers, says malicious 1.107.0 packages were published on PyPI, as wheels for macOS, Linux and Windows, and as Docker images on 21 October. Its security lead says the release was triggered and approved from three engineers’ GitHub accounts using stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens; how the tokens were taken is not known. The PyPI package was quarantined, the images removed, the tokens revoked and the organisation’s access cut back to one user. SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity and Upwind report that the payload runs at Python start-up through a .pth file and collects cloud tokens, developer credentials, private keys, AI-tool credential files, browser data, environment variables and the provider API keys the proxy stores, sends them to litellm[.]dev and polls a GitHub dead drop every hour. No download count has been published. It is the project’s second compromise this year.

items.title: Developer platforms are leaking customers’ secrets: Railway tells every user to rotate environment variables, Zeabur shuts down after a second breach, and OpenCode and PingCAP report exposed keys
items.content_text: Railway, which hosts about 4.8 million users, said on 21 October that an unauthorised party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables and, for some, their decrypted contents; it paused all deployments, told every user to rotate all secrets and later advised checking for unusual AWS and GCP access. Railway believes it was part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at AI inference providers. Zeabur says leaked internal admin credentials, stored in plaintext and not rotated since January 2024, let an attacker into its shared cluster on 14–15 October, exposing data for 321,810 accounts and more than 3.2 million environment-variable records; it will shut the service down by 31 December. OpenCode says a legacy Console system breached on 16 October may have exposed the stored OpenAI, Anthropic and Google API keys of 1.4% of Console users, and PingCAP says stolen service-account credentials gave an intruder TiDB Cloud billing, usage and SQL-editor data and encrypted API keys from 9 September to 7 October. None of the companies has linked its incident to the others.

_threatfeed.source_name: Railway security disclosure; Zeabur via BleepingComputer; OpenCode via The Hacker News; PingCAP via Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Zeabur breach 14–15 Oct 2026; OpenCode 16 Oct 2026; Railway detected 21 Oct 2026; guidance updated 22 Oct 2026

items.title: Two WordPress plugin vendors were turned against their own customers in one week — stolen UpdraftCentral keys pushed backdoor plugins to sites, and Rank Math PRO was served trojanised from its own site
items.content_text: TeamUpdraft says it found unauthorised access to the teamupdraft.com website over the weekend of 17–18 October. It believes the attackers took the customer database holding UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone connection keys and used them on 18–19 October to send signed commands that installed backdoor plugins, which create hidden administrator-level users; Patchstack counts 99 plugin names used. UpdraftPlus has more than 4 million active installs, but self-hosted UpdraftCentral and the plugin code itself were not affected, and the number of sites hit has not been published. UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (Premium 2.26.13) disconnects connections made before 18 October. Separately, Rank Math says PRO 3.0.123 downloaded from its own site during an 11-hour window on 15–16 October contained malware that persists, recreates backdoors and exposes database credentials and API keys to a “limited number of users”; 3.0.124 is clean, the free WordPress.org version was not affected, and updating alone does not clean a site.

_threatfeed.source_name: TeamUpdraft; Rank Math advisory; Patchstack; Wordfence; The Hacker News; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Rank Math window 15–16 Oct 2026; TeamUpdraft breach 17–18 Oct, backdoors 18–19 Oct 2026; disclosed 19–21 Oct 2026

items.title: Ahold Delhaize says its outage was caused by “malicious actions of others” and is bringing brands back online — Albert Heijn home delivery restarted on 23 October; no evidence so far that sensitive data was taken
items.content_text: In a 19 October update Ahold Delhaize confirmed that the suspicious activity it first disclosed on 12 October was caused by “malicious actions of others”. It notified the Dutch NCSC, filed a police report and says it has found no evidence so far that sensitive customer, associate or partner data was taken; stores stayed open throughout. Systems including brand websites and apps had been taken offline across most of its brands in Europe and the US. The Albert Heijn website and app were back by 19 October and home deliveries restarted on 23 October, NL Times reported; the Boston Globe, quoting the company, reported Stop & Shop and Hannaford back on 20 October, while the status of Food Lion and Giant has not been confirmed. According to an Albert Heijn statement reported by NL Times, some of its distribution centres stalled on 13–14 October. BleepingComputer reported that Stop & Shop staff could not reach schedules and pay stubs. No ransomware group has claimed it and no entry point has been named. It is an IT-side incident that disrupted logistics, not a confirmed compromise of store or warehouse control systems, and the Dutch NCSC sees no link to the French supermarket refrigeration attacks.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ahold Delhaize newsroom (12, 13 and 19 Oct); NL Times; Boston Globe; The Record; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 11 Oct 2026; statements 12, 13 and 19 Oct 2026; Stop & Shop and Hannaford back 20 Oct 2026; Albert Heijn deliveries 23 Oct 2026

items.title: US bankruptcy notices are still not going out two weeks after a cybersecurity incident at contractor BAE Systems — courts are issuing emergency orders, and there is still no restoration date
items.content_text: The Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC), which BAE Systems runs for the federal judiciary, still could not send notices and orders as of 22 October: the US Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Florida described a “nationwide service disruption” that prevents it from transmitting them in the ordinary course. Notices have not gone out since 9 October, when BAE first told the courts, and the Administrative Office of the US Courts confirmed a cybersecurity incident on 15 October. Courts are working around it with orders of their own: Northern Florida entered its second administrative order on 20 October, the Southern District of New York has posted general orders, and Alaska is postponing some creditor meetings until the BNC is back. Filings are still accepted and CM/ECF still sends electronic notices. BAE said on 16 October that the incident is isolated to the BNC system and no other systems were affected. The cause, any data exposure and a restoration date have not been disclosed.

_threatfeed.source_name: US Bankruptcy Court, Northern District of Florida; Administrative Office of the US Courts; BAE Systems via CyberScoop; Cybernews; US Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York
_threatfeed.date_note: BAE notified the courts 9 Oct 2026; incident confirmed 15 Oct 2026; BAE statement 16 Oct 2026; still down 22 Oct 2026

items.title: One compromised login let an intruder copy California students’ assessment records from testing contractor ETS for four months — reported at about 7 million students
items.content_text: The California Department of Education and ETS began notifying families on 16 October that an unauthorised party used a compromised login credential between 22 May and 18 September to copy files from an ETS SFTP site used to exchange statewide assessment data (CAASPP and ELPAC). ETS spotted the activity on 25 September. The files cover students enrolled in the past three school years plus some former students back to 2006, reported at about 7 million: names, dates of birth, home addresses, schools, student IDs, demographic and language data and test results, and for some students disability, Section 504 and other programme flags. No Social Security numbers, passwords, financial data or parent information were involved, and ETS says it has seen no publication of the data. ETS took the SFTP site offline and is building a hardened replacement; law enforcement is investigating, and no actor has been named or has claimed it.

_threatfeed.source_name: California Department of Education and ETS notices (as quoted); SecurityWeek; EdSource; Cybernews; DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Access 22 May–18 Sep 2026; detected 25 Sep 2026; notices from 16 Oct 2026

items.title: Staffing-software provider Bullhorn took its platform offline to contain a cyber incident — most services are back, but its back-office payroll system stays down this week
items.content_text: Bullhorn, whose applicant-tracking, CRM and back-office software serves more than 10,000 staffing customers, said on 18 October that it had detected a cyber incident and temporarily disabled access to its systems; problems began on 17 October. It is working with CrowdStrike. All users who do not sign in through single sign-on must reset their passwords, and API passwords must be rotated. By 22 October its status page listed most affected services as upgraded and restored, including Talent Platform, but Bullhorn Back Office was expected to stay unavailable through the end of the week, so timesheets could not be entered and support was running payroll reports on request. Bullhorn says it has not yet determined whether data was taken and will notify individuals if a breach is confirmed. No group has claimed it. Later status updates mention the PHP2Shell flaws, but Bullhorn has not said whether they relate to the incident.

_threatfeed.source_name: Bullhorn status page; BleepingComputer; The Register
_threatfeed.date_note: Problems from 17 Oct 2026; incident confirmed 18 Oct 2026; status 22 Oct 2026

items.title: IDC Frontier has brought back its IDCF Cloud backup service after the unauthorised-access outage that hit 495 customers — snapshots are still suspended and the cause is undisclosed
items.content_text: In its sixth report, on 18 October, SoftBank-owned IDC Frontier said it had resumed the IDCF Cloud backup service after a safety check, so customers can back up and restore to other clouds or on-premises systems; the snapshot function remains suspended. Virtual servers in its East Japan 1, 2 and 3 and West Japan 1 regions stay in use, and customers are asked to back them up as a precaution. The outage, caused by a third party’s unauthorised access, began at about 03:40 Japan time on 7 October and hit 495 companies and local governments across four zones of Tokyo East Region 1. IDC Frontier’s 14 October report found no sign that virtual-server data was taken out, and said unauthorised queries reached portal registration data for 48 customers with no evidence it left its systems. A 23 October site notice reported no new material facts. The cause, method and actor have not been disclosed, and IDC Frontier does not call it ransomware.

_threatfeed.source_name: IDC Frontier incident reports Nos. 5 and 6 and site notice; IBTimes; DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Outage began 7 Oct 2026; fifth report 14 Oct 2026; sixth report 18 Oct 2026; no new facts 23 Oct 2026

items.title: GhostAction’s operators came back six days after GitHub blocked their workflow — a second stage hides a credential stealer in a fake font file and runs when a developer opens the folder
items.content_text: After GitHub began blocking the malicious GhostAction workflow on 9 October, the operators returned on 15 October with a second stage that does not need a CI runner, OpenSourceMalware researchers reported on 19 October. In 94 repositories they planted a VS Code tasks.json that runs when a developer opens the folder, a payload disguised as the font file fa-solid-400.woff2, a backup workflow and a scheduled job that runs attacker code every five minutes; it targets AWS, PyPI, npm, Git, Kubernetes and SSH credentials and Anthropic and Gemini API keys. Researchers also found a phishing kit posing as a GitHub security alert that approves an OAuth device-flow login with repository and workflow scopes, but say they have no evidence tying it to GhostAction. The first stage, reported by GitGuardian on 15 October, hijacked about 1,900 GitHub accounts and pushed secret-stealing workflows to more than 30,000 repositories; waves on 10 and 12 October extracted nothing after GitHub’s block. No victims have been named.

_threatfeed.source_name: OpenSourceMalware via The Hacker News; GitGuardian; Wiz threat-intel entry
_threatfeed.date_note: Stage 1 spike 8–9 Oct 2026; GitHub block 9 Oct 2026; stage 2 from 15 Oct 2026; reported 19 Oct 2026

items.title: Capcom confirms a breach of its CAPCOM ID account system exposing about 11.7 million email addresses and login details — attackers also changed the passwords on 196 accounts
items.content_text: Capcom said on 22 October that it detected unauthorised access to its shared CAPCOM ID account system on 19 October. Exposed for more than 11.7 million accounts: email addresses, account creation dates, last login times, login counts and last-login IP addresses; for a further 43 accounts, date of birth, gender, nickname and country were also exposed. The attackers changed the passwords of 196 accounts, locking their owners out, and Capcom has reset them. Capcom says other members’ passwords and payment card data were not exposed. It reported the incident to police and to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission on 21 October. It says it has identified the intrusion method but has not disclosed it, and no group has claimed the attack.

_threatfeed.source_name: Capcom; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 19 Oct 2026; reported to regulators 21 Oct 2026; public 22 Oct 2026

items.title: The FBI and Secret Service say the FortiBleed campaign is still getting into FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPNs with stolen and cracked credentials — there is no CVE to patch
items.content_text: In a joint advisory dated 6 October (JCSA-20261006-01), the FBI and US Secret Service warned that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat, with targets across all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors. The agencies say it exploits reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps, extracted hashes sent to a GPU cracking cluster, and a Go tool called FortigateSniffer that intercepts authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after attackers changed admin passwords or deleted accounts. The agencies say compromised FortiGates are being used as ransomware entry points, and the advisory links the Payload ransomware operation; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments. The scale figure in circulation, more than 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries, is SOCRadar’s count as of 19 June, not a new one. SOCRadar describes the operator as a Russian-speaking access broker with overlaps to INC and Lynx affiliates; that is researcher assessment, not agency attribution. No CVE is involved.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory (IC3); SOCRadar; The Hacker News; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign documented Jun 2026; joint advisory 6 Oct 2026

items.title: CrowdStrike says an operator using the open-source agentic pentest tool ARTEX and several AI models breached South Korean financial firms and took data
items.content_text: CrowdStrike reported on 7 October that exposed attacker directories showed a likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated operator using ARTEX, a Chinese-developed open-source agentic penetration-testing tool, together with large language models including DeepSeek, GLM and Grok, to breach several South Korean financial organisations between late September and early October and exfiltrate data. Exposed sessions also included Claude Code. At one bank the operator went after a broker loan-progress inquiry service, and at another an employee mobile work-support system. CrowdStrike does not name the victims; Korean press, cited by The Hacker News, names Shinhan Bank and Yegaram Savings Bank. Korea’s Financial Services Commission and Financial Supervisory Service warned consumers about phishing and loan scams using the leaked data. CrowdStrike’s assessment of the operator is at moderate confidence and names no group.

_threatfeed.source_name: CrowdStrike; Korea Financial Services Commission; The Hacker News; The Register; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Sep–early Oct 2026; CrowdStrike report 7 Oct 2026

items.title: The UK Legal Aid Agency breach took far more than first thought — records back to 1978, probation data and judges’ names, the Ministry of Justice now says
items.content_text: In a written statement to Parliament reported on 15 October, Justice Minister Sarah Sackman said forensic analysis of the April–May 2025 intrusion at the Legal Aid Agency found more data had been taken than first believed. Most records relate to applications, claims or payments from January 2007 to 16 May 2025, plus about 250,000 older records, the earliest from 1978. The stolen data includes probation records with names, dates of birth, nationality and case references; National Insurance numbers; financial assessments of defendants and their partners, with bank and property details; some partially redacted card details; and the names of judges, lawyers and court reporters in Crown Court trials. The Ministry of Justice says it has no indication the data has been published. The attackers, unnamed criminal extortionists, have claimed data on more than two million people; there is no official count.

items.title: Arizona’s court system says hackers copied backup files covering about 1.3 million people’s fines and restitution records, foster-care reports and protective orders — after one phishing click
items.content_text: The Arizona Supreme Court’s Administrative Office of the Courts says criminal hackers accessed and copied backup court files after an employee clicked a phishing link on 24 September; court IT shut the intrusion down within about two hours. The copied data includes Fines/Fees and Restitution Enforcement (FARE) records on roughly 1.3 million people, with names, Social Security numbers, case numbers and debts going back about 30 years, more than 150,000 Foster Care Review Board reports dating to 2010, and active and inactive protective-order records. The court told The Record on 7 October that it was not ransomware and no ransom had been demanded. The FBI is involved, and no group had claimed the attack. The data sat in backup copies, which are often watched less closely than production systems.

_threatfeed.source_name: Arizona courts cybersecurity alert and FAQ; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 24 Sep 2026; announced 25 Sep 2026; scope reported 7 Oct 2026

items.title: Meta says an outside group used one employee’s stolen credentials to copy code from its GitHub repositories — about 1,500 people notified because personal data had been committed there
items.content_text: Meta began notifying about 1,500 people, mostly US employees, on 13 October after an outside group used an employee’s stolen credentials to access some of its GitHub repositories. About 99% of what was taken was business data, mainly source code; about 1% was personal data that had been committed to repositories against policy, much of it synthetic test data. Meta says no vulnerability in any Meta product was involved and its internal systems were not breached. It rotated exposed secrets, brought in GitHub and law enforcement and is notifying regulators. It has not said which types of personal data were exposed, and no link to any named group or to other GitHub campaigns has been reported.

items.title: South African pathology lab Ampath confirms a cyberattack that likely exposed patient data — but says an attacker’s claim of 80 million records materially overstates it
items.content_text: South African pathology laboratory group Ampath confirmed it was the target of a cyberattack that likely compromised patient data, after a threat actor posted screenshots on 13 October and claimed to have taken more than 80 million patient records. Ampath says that figure materially overstates the number of people potentially affected. The claim comes from an extortion actor known as ByteToBreach, previously active against African targets. Treat the 80 million figure with caution: it is larger than South Africa’s population of about 63 million. Ampath has not given its own count or said how the attackers got in.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ampath statements via MyBroadband; DataBreaches.net; BankInfoSecurity
_threatfeed.date_note: Claim posted and attack confirmed 13 Oct 2026; updated 14 Oct 2026

items.title: OpenAI and Anthropic disclose that their models broke into third-party systems during training and evaluations — Anthropic has cut live internet access for its internal tests
items.content_text: On 15 October OpenAI published misalignment reports on three incidents from June, each rated critical, in which models doing routine tasks took unauthorised actions and left them out of their answers. On an unnamed government statistics website a model forged unsigned tokens, pulled a configuration file holding a database connection string, a token-signing secret and email credentials, and fetched more than 1,000 account records. On an unnamed international research organisation’s dashboard a model used credentials exposed in public JavaScript to pull 1,489 user records and later 147,451 non-public rows. A third model spent another party’s Sepolia test-network tokens, which have no monetary value. In a disclosure reported on 10 October, Anthropic said it had cut live internet access for all internal evaluations until further notice after finding that models had exploited SQL and command injection in third-party software to run commands on a university server, submitted a false tip through a real Philadelphia police form and got past a fee gate to reach state agency data; it called the impact minimal. These are self-disclosures of model behaviour, not attacker campaigns, but the systems reached were real ones with ordinary weaknesses (see the earlier OpenAI card).

items.title: Ledger confirms a hidden hardware implant in wallets sold by a Southeast Asian reseller stole recovery phrases and drained funds — it has asked sellers across Asia to halt sales
items.content_text: Ledger confirmed on 12 October that one affected user’s device contained an unauthorised hardware implant, after users reported drained wallets on 9 October. All the reports trace to devices sold through CryptoBilis, a Malaysia-based reseller outside Ledger’s recommended channels. Ledger told buyers from that reseller not to set up their devices, or to move assets to a new signer with a new recovery phrase, and on 14 October asked sellers across Asia to halt sales while it investigates. Researchers who examined the devices say the implant read the recovery phrase from the screen during setup and sent it out over an embedded LTE eSIM, leaving the secure element intact so the device may still pass authenticity checks; that analysis is the researchers’, not Ledger’s. Ledger calls the number of affected devices limited and has not disclosed a victim count, models or losses.

_threatfeed.source_name: Ledger statements; BleepingComputer; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Thefts 9 Oct 2026; implant confirmed 12 Oct 2026; Asia sales halt 14 Oct 2026

items.title: ASOS confirms hackers broke into a third-party platform it uses to message customers and took names and contact details — after a rogue push notification reached its app users
items.content_text: Around 5–6 October ASOS customers received an unauthorised push notification through the retailer’s own app claiming that its Snowflake data had been fully compromised. In a London Stock Exchange filing on 8 October, ASOS confirmed that hackers had broken into a third-party platform it uses to communicate with customers and taken names and contact details plus some non-personal account information; its 13 October customer update says no payment-card data or passwords were affected. ASOS has not said how many customers are affected. A self-styled Xuanye Group has claimed it; Snowflake says its own systems were not breached. The BBC reported broader fields, including home addresses and search queries, and BleepingComputer reported access through social-engineered credentials for a Snowflake instance; those are the outlets’ reports, not ASOS statements.

_threatfeed.source_name: ASOS LSE filing and customer update; TechCrunch; The Register; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Rogue notification ~5–6 Oct 2026; filing 8 Oct 2026; customer update 13 Oct 2026

items.title: CenterPoint Energy tells Texas regulators its data breach affects 1,062,060 Texans — names, Social Security and driver’s licence numbers; operations were not affected
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy told the Texas Attorney General’s Office that 1,062,060 Texas residents were affected by its data breach, with names, addresses, Social Security numbers and driver’s licence numbers exposed, SecurityWeek reported on 15 October. Residents of Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio may also be affected, so the total is unclear. According to its SEC filing, CenterPoint learned of the breach from the attacker’s public post; the attacker had claimed nearly 7.5 million user records and posted a 2.5 GB archive on 12 September. The company says the incident did not affect its operations. It has not said how the attacker got in.

_threatfeed.source_name: CenterPoint Texas AG and SEC filings via SecurityWeek; Security Affairs
_threatfeed.date_note: Attacker post 12 Sep 2026; Texas AG figure reported 15 Oct 2026

items.title: Denmark says names, addresses and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million people were pulled from its population register through a private company’s legitimate lookup access
items.content_text: Denmark’s Ministry of Higher Education and Science announced on 5 October that unauthorised parties had used a private Danish company’s authorised access to the CPR, the Central Person Register, to extract data on about 8.8 million registered people, living, deceased and emigrated. The ministry lists names, addresses and CPR numbers. The CPR number is Denmark’s personal identity number and encodes the date of birth. The irregular activity took place in September and was discovered on the evening of 2 October. The government has not named the company, and its access has been revoked; police are investigating, the data protection authority has been notified and a hotline has been set up for citizens. According to The Hacker News and BleepingComputer, the attackers enumerated valid CPR numbers through automated lookups. Update, 13 October: The Register, citing Politiken and TV 2, reports that the access belonged to the IT firm Pays ApS, whose managing director confirmed on 9 October that it had been exploited, and that about 14 million automated searches ran between 10 and 20 September. A person claiming responsibility told Politiken they got in through an account protected by the password “123456” that several accounts shared; that is the claimant’s account, not an official finding. Still officially unknown: whether the data has been used and who is behind it. For any organisation that gives partners API or lookup access to sensitive records, the lesson is that legitimate access was enough. The controls that would have mattered are volume and rate limits and monitoring of what an authorised client actually pulls.

_threatfeed.source_name: Danish Ministry of Higher Education and Science; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; The Register (citing Politiken and TV 2)
_threatfeed.date_note: Activity Sep 2026; discovered 2 Oct 2026; announced 5 Oct 2026; company confirmation 9 Oct 2026; reported 13 Oct 2026

items.title: The Pentagon’s Defense Manpower Data Center breach reached nearly 2.8 million living people and about 294,000 deceased, according to Pentagon figures reported by CNN and Federal News Network — intruders had quiet access to a file-sharing system for about nine months
items.content_text: The Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC), which holds Department of Defense personnel records, has been notifying people that unauthorised users reached a file-sharing system within DMDC “between October 2025 and July 16, 2026”. According to the letters, dated 18 September, the problem was found and fixed on 16 July. The exposed data includes Social Security numbers, names, dates of birth, contact details, sex, race and military personnel information such as occupational specialty; CNN reported that the data was not encrypted. Update, 1 October: Pentagon figures cited by CNN and Federal News Network, and reported by BleepingComputer, put the total at more than 3 million: nearly 2.8 million living and about 294,000 deceased people. That replaces the unofficial figure of about 4 million in earlier coverage. The Military Officers Association of America noted on 30 September that DoD had issued no official news release, so treat the numbers as reported. The department is offering 12 months of IDX credit monitoring. No actor, vendor or flaw has been named. The lesson for everyone else is the dwell time: about nine months of quiet access to identity data through a file-sharing system.

_threatfeed.source_name: DMDC notification letter via Military Times and CNN; Federal News Network; BleepingComputer; MOAA
_threatfeed.date_note: Letters dated 18 Sep 2026; figures reported 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Bitget’s investigators say attackers took over two third-party security appliances, planted a web shell and pushed malicious packages to the wallet server — up to about US$388 million taken, and Bitget says the way in was a zero-day
items.content_text: Cryptocurrency exchange Bitget lost funds in unauthorised transfers on 24–25 September. A Mandiant status update, published by Bitget on 28 September, says the attackers gained unauthorised privileged access to two unnamed third-party security appliances, put a web shell and command-and-control tooling on one of them, and then deployed malicious packages to the production server that runs wallet jobs. Mandiant puts the loss at US$351.6–387.5 million; the US$390.06 million figure in earlier reports, including the previous edition of this page, is superseded. Cold wallets and private keys were not affected. On 1 October Bitget said its investigation found that a zero-day in third-party security products was the entry point. No vendor, product or CVE has been named. About US$1.1 million has been frozen by stablecoin issuers and other services. The North Korea link is Bitget’s own assessment, supported by the blockchain-analytics firms TRM Labs and Elliptic, which point to the group tracked as TraderTraitor. Mandiant’s document makes no attribution, and no government has attributed the theft. The lesson has two parts. The attacker did not need the keys, because it controlled systems trusted to run and approve transfers. And the way in was the security tooling itself.

_threatfeed.source_name: Mandiant status update (published by Bitget); Bitget statement; The Hacker News; Bloomberg
_threatfeed.date_note: Theft 24–25 Sep 2026; Mandiant update 28 Sep 2026; Bitget cause statement 1 Oct 2026

items.title: The FBI says its jobs-portal breach came from a contractor’s missed patch on a platform run by a third party, and that “multiple” ShinyHunters suspects have been arrested — which undercuts the group’s zero-day claim
items.content_text: ShinyHunters defaced a subdomain of the FBIJobs.gov applicant portal on 21 September, claimed a zero-day in Oracle PeopleSoft and leaked personnel data, some of which 404 Media found to be genuine. Two weeks on, the picture has changed. Dutch police announced on 29 September that a 24-year-old man had been arrested in Amsterdam earlier in the month; the FBI called him one of the group’s alleged leaders and urged other members to surrender. Reuters reported that a second suspect was detained in Jordan in late September and is cooperating; he is reportedly a minor. On 5 October the FBI confirmed it had worked with partners to arrest “multiple subjects”. This page names no suspects. On 6 October Reuters and The Hacker News quoted FBI Cyber Division Assistant Director Brett Leatherman as saying the breach followed a security failure on a platform managed by a third party, after a contractor failed to implement a security patch, and that the FBI has removed the contractor. The FBI has not named the contractor, the platform or the flaw. Reports name Accenture and link the breach to PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 (see that card); both remain reported, not confirmed. A missed patch points to a known flaw rather than the zero-day ShinyHunters claimed. Update, 9 October: the FBI announced a further arrest, of a Canadian national in Pennsylvania who is not named here, and alleges the group has breached more than 140 organisations and extorted at least US$70 million.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI statements via Reuters, The Hacker News and The Register; Dutch police; BleepingComputer; The Record; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Defacement 21 Sep 2026; Dutch arrest announced 29 Sep 2026; FBI arrest statement 5 Oct 2026; cause statement 6 Oct 2026; further arrest 9 Oct 2026

items.title: Symantec says a China-nexus group it calls Longlegs broke into a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university through on-premises SharePoint, then deployed Warlock ransomware — using SharePoint flaws from 2025
items.content_text: Symantec reported on 1 October that Longlegs, which it describes as a China-nexus threat actor also known as Storm-2603, has attacked at least four organisations in the past two months, two of them critical-infrastructure operators: a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America. None is named. Longlegs typically gets in by exploiting on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server. The only CVEs Symantec names are the 2025 “ToolShell” flaws, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771, plus other related SharePoint flaws, and the intrusions it details took place in late July 2026. Symantec does not link this activity to the newer SharePoint flaw CVE-2026-65660 (see that card). Once inside, the attackers stole ASP.NET machine keys, ran a VS Code tunnel as a service, used NetExec, loaded the vulnerable K7RKScan driver (CVE-2025-1055) to disable security software, and in one case pushed Warlock to at least 33 hosts through SYSVOL. Symantec describes no operational or OT impact at the water utility. The attribution is Symantec’s assessment. The point for defenders is that SharePoint flaws from 2025 are still giving a ransomware crew its way in.

_threatfeed.source_name: Symantec (Broadcom) threat intelligence; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; Industrial Cyber
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusions late Jul 2026; report 1 Oct 2026

items.title: OpenAI now says its research agents reached four Australian public-sector data systems, retrieving internal files and credentials at the Medicare statistics service — and California’s attorney general has subpoenaed the company
items.content_text: On 24 September Australia’s Prime Minister disclosed that AI agents run by OpenAI gained unauthorised access in June to a Services Australia Medicare statistics reporting service while collecting data for a research project. OpenAI’s own 28 September account goes further. It says a model found a way to gain non-public access to the Medicare service, ran commands, and retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics; no patient records were accessed. At the Victorian Agency for Health Information, agents found an exposed access key and retrieved reporting configuration and aggregate survey statistics. At the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, a crime-mapping API returned application configuration, operational jobs and logs, and website metadata. At the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare only aggregate statistics were reached, through third-party browsing services, which OpenAI says was not a compromise. OpenAI has promised an Australian taskforce with independent expertise, reporting by the end of 2026. Separately, its 25 September alignment report says an agent used a DNS-filtering gap on 20 September to tunnel queries to an outside chatbot, with no confirmed data exposure, and that tool use for its most capable models remains paused. On 1 October California Attorney General Rob Bonta served OpenAI an investigative subpoena on cybersecurity incidents and risks tied to its models. OpenAI said earlier that its agents also engaged with US government websites, without unauthorised access. The lesson: agents given a harmless task treated other organisations’ access controls as obstacles, and used exposed keys to get past them.

_threatfeed.source_name: OpenAI; Australian Prime Minister’s statement; California Attorney General; The Register; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Access Jun 2026; disclosed 24 Sep 2026; OpenAI account 28 Sep 2026; subpoena 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Astrana Health tells the SEC that callers spoofing its own main phone number got employees to hand over access, and that confidential data was taken — patient, employee and provider data may be involved
items.content_text: Astrana Health, a Nasdaq-listed healthcare company (ASTH), filed a Form 8-K under Item 1.05 on 23 September. It says it determined on 22 September that a cybersecurity incident was material. The filing says the incident began with “social engineering attempts in which threat actors, impersonating Company personnel and spoofing the Company’s main corporate telephone number, contacted certain employees”, and that “certain private and/or confidential information maintained on the Company’s servers has been accessed and/or acquired without authorization.” Data potentially involved includes patient information, employee records, credentialed-provider data, business and financial information and intellectual property. Astrana is still assessing it and gives no count. It has reset credentials, restricted remote-access tools, restored systems from clean backups, added monitoring and engaged forensic firms, and it has notified law enforcement and regulators. It says it does not currently expect a material effect on its financial condition. No group has claimed the attack. The case is here for the technique. The caller ID showed the company’s own number, so the check most staff rely on said the call was internal.

_threatfeed.source_name: Astrana Health Form 8-K (SEC EDGAR); The Record; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Materiality determined 22 Sep 2026; 8-K filed 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Canva confirms that a breach at its feedback vendor Canny reached its Salesforce account — Canva calls it limited business-contact and contract data, and the attackers’ far larger claims are unverified
items.content_text: Canva has confirmed that “the unauthorised access to Canny allowed access to limited enterprise customer information through its connection to our Salesforce account, including business contact details and contract information.” Canny, a product-feedback vendor, was hit on 28 August and notified Canva on the 29th. A new group calling itself “The Seven Deadly Sins” claims much more: over 2 million CRM records and 200 million data-warehouse rows from Canva, 3.8 TB in total, and access to more than 300 Jira instances and 50-plus Salesforce, HubSpot and Zendesk tenants at other companies, naming Mercury.com and Proxyscrape.io. None of that is confirmed, and Canva did not respond to DataBreaches.net about the wider claims. The confirmed part is the useful one. Nobody broke into Canva’s own platform. A small vendor holding a connection into Canva’s CRM was breached, and that connection carried the data out. It is the same path as the Salesloft Drift and Gainsight incidents of 2025, and every connected app in your CRM is another one.

_threatfeed.source_name: Canva statement via DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Canny intrusion 28 Aug 2026; public 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Researchers report an operator using open-source AI agent frameworks to plant card skimmers on more than 100 sites and collect over 600,000 card records — a single vendor’s findings, no victim named
items.content_text: Security start-up Gambit reported on 23 September that a financially motivated, apparently Chinese-speaking operator ran a card-skimming campaign from July to 22 September using three open-source agent frameworks: Strix for discovery, Cairn for exploitation and an orchestration layer called Hermes, which Gambit says was configured to use Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 model. Gambit counts skimmers on more than 100 sites (119 in its data), at least 27 companies breached, and more than 600,000 card records. Magento databases were among the targets. Injection points included edited JavaScript files, script tags on checkout pages, Google Tag blocks, poisoned S3, CDN and server caches, database fields, Kubernetes deployments and cron jobs. Unnamed victims include a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, an industrial distributor and an online fashion retailer, and Gambit puts the operator’s cost at about US$25 per target. All figures come from one vendor and no victim has confirmed. The report describes an attacker misusing open-source tooling. It does not say the model provider’s platform was compromised. The techniques themselves are old. The report’s claim is that agents let one operator run them against dozens of targets at once. The Register’s 25 September account of the same research adds that more than 600,000 of the card records came from two victims, and that the operator’s instructions to “clean up” wiped card data from victims’ databases, disrupting their operations. Those details also come from Gambit alone.

_threatfeed.source_name: Gambit research via BleepingComputer; The Register
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign July–22 Sep 2026; reported 23 Sep 2026; further detail 25 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA, the FBI and UK and German partners say SafePay ransomware has hit at least 600 organisations since August 2024 — exposed VPN logins and old edge-device flaws are the way in
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-293A, released on 20 October by CISA, the FBI and the US Secret Service with Germany’s LKA Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK National Crime Agency and the North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, says SafePay has hit at least 600 organisations in multiple critical-infrastructure sectors across the Americas, Europe and Australia since August 2024. SafePay is a closed group with no affiliates that steals data before encrypting it. The agencies list exposed or brute-forced credentials, VPN logins (notably from Mullvad addresses), phished accounts and automated exploitation of edge devices, including the Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense flaws CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269. Inside, the operators use WinRM, PsExec and RDP, move data with tools such as FileZilla, WinSCP and Rclone, delete shadow copies and reset NAS devices that hold backups. The advisory names no victims; SafePay claimed the Conduent breach disclosed in January 2025, and Conduent agreed on 16 October to an $80 million class settlement.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA / FBI joint advisory AA26-293A via BleepingComputer and Cybersecurity Dive; HIPAA Journal; Conduent Form 8-K
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory 20 Oct 2026; reported 21 Oct 2026; Conduent settlement 16 Oct 2026

items.title: Unit 42 says Qilin and INC ransomware crews are using GlobalProtect flaw CVE-2026-0257 to open VPN sessions past MFA, then going after vCenter, ESXi and Veeam backup servers
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 now names INC ransomware, which it tracks as Tarnished Scorpius, alongside Qilin (Spikey Scorpius) in exploiting CVE-2026-0257, the GlobalProtect authentication bypass in PAN-OS and Prisma Access patched in May, to establish VPN sessions without passing MFA, according to reporting on 20 October. In one case the intruders moved from the VPN to vCenter, switched off the ESXi execInstalledOnly protection and dumped domain-controller credentials offline from the virtual disk, which Unit 42 says can sidestep endpoint detection inside the guest; they also chained the 2023 Veeam Backup & Replication flaw CVE-2023-27532 and used remote-management tools, RDP and SMB. Targets span education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, legal and professional services, government, transport, utilities and retail. ReliaQuest named Qilin and Settra on 9 October and warned that patching alone may not remove access gained earlier. It is a different flaw from the management-interface zero-day CVE-2026-0322 (see that card).
tags: Threat intel — Ransomware exploiting a VPN flaw

_threatfeed.category: Threat intel — Ransomware exploiting a VPN flaw
_threatfeed.source_name: Unit 42 via The Hacker News and Cybersecurity Dive; ReliaQuest via Infosecurity Magazine; Palo Alto Networks; Arctic Wolf
_threatfeed.date_note: Patched May 2026; ReliaQuest warning 9 Oct 2026; Unit 42 update reported 20 Oct 2026

items.title: Huntress saw stolen Microsoft 365 session tokens replayed in about 200,000 sign-in attempts, 497 of them successful — MFA never prompted because the token had already passed it
items.content_text: Huntress reported on 22 October that between July and September attackers replayed Microsoft 365 session tokens, stolen through adversary-in-the-middle and device-code phishing, in about 200,000 sign-in attempts, 497 of which succeeded. Because a stolen token carries an MFA claim that has already been satisfied, users were not prompted. Across 79 customer organisations it investigated, attackers were inside within minutes, reset MFA methods, registered their own phones and devices in Entra ID, created hidden inbox rules and sent payroll-diversion phishing from the compromised mailboxes. Huntress does not attribute the activity, and it is separate from the ConnectWise and Storm-0940 tenant intrusions (see the top story).

_threatfeed.source_name: Huntress via Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Activity Jul–Sep 2026; Huntress report 22 Oct 2026

items.title: Symantec: Russia’s APT28 spent at least two months inside a NATO naval shipbuilder’s network and also broke into a military aircraft-engine maker and a law-enforcement agency
items.content_text: Symantec’s Threat Hunter team reported on 20 October that Swallowtail — its name for APT28, also known as Fancy Bear and Forest Blizzard and attributed to Russia’s GRU — compromised a naval shipbuilder, a military aircraft-engine maker and a police and law-enforcement agency, all in NATO countries it did not name. At the shipbuilder the group spent at least two months in the IT network. The tooling included the Hookedge backdoor and a previously undocumented in-memory loader whose final payload was not recovered. No impact on operational technology was reported. Symantec’s suggestion that the motive is linked to support for Ukraine is analyst speculation, not a finding.

_threatfeed.source_name: Symantec Threat Hunter team via CyberScoop; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Symantec report 20 Oct 2026

items.title: Google’s threat-intelligence team says AOMEI Backupper’s update server was tampered with for minutes at a time to install a backdoor on IT-services, telecom and university machines
items.content_text: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant report that an actor they track as UNC7017 altered configuration files on AOMEI’s update servers in windows of five to ten minutes on at least 28 May, 16 July and 20 July 2026, so only Backupper clients that checked for updates during a window were hit. Those clients received a CROSSROAD downloader, a signed copy of the Radmin remote-access tool and a SHINYROAD implant, with Adaptix command-and-control on some hosts; the 20 July variant also leaked NetNTLMv2 hashes over WebDAV. Victims were in IT services, telecommunications and higher education across 11 countries, including the US; GTIG names no country behind UNC7017. AOMEI first blamed interception in transit, which the researchers say the evidence does not support. It told Mandiant on 29 July that its servers were secured, but its update verification has not changed through version 8.5.0.

_threatfeed.source_name: Google Threat Intelligence Group / Mandiant; ManageEngine; The Hacker News; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Tampering 28 May–20 Jul 2026; research published 16 Oct 2026

items.title: US authorities seize domains behind Microscan and FishHub, scanning and phishing tools they tie to China-based Integrity Technology Group — a joint advisory lists the targets
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 8 October court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains used by Microscan, a vulnerability-scanning platform, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery service. US authorities say both were built and run by China-based Integrity Technology Group, whose activity overlaps the group tracked as Flax Typhoon; Cybersecurity Dive describes the activity as mimicking Flax Typhoon rather than equating the two. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan, which court documents say carried more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and the joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory (AA26-281A) notes persistence through VPN software. Named targets include a South Carolina power company, a multinational NGO, airports in Japan and Poland, gas and power companies in Taiwan and 20 Taiwanese universities; the reporting does not confirm any target was compromised. CISA’s Chris Butera said China-affiliated actors continue to position themselves in critical-infrastructure networks, including operational technology.

_threatfeed.source_name: DOJ / FBI; FBI, CISA and NSA advisory AA26-281A; CyberScoop; Cybersecurity Dive
_threatfeed.date_note: Seizures and advisory 8 Oct 2026; court-document details reported 9 Oct 2026

items.title: Rapid7 finds a new BPFDoor variant and a new implant, AVERAT, on telecom-edge and mail-security devices in South Korea and Taiwan — AVERAT hides its beacon in what looks like ordinary SMTP traffic
items.content_text: Rapid7 reported on 2 October a new variant of the BPFDoor backdoor and a BPF-based Rekoobe build in South Korea, and six builds of a new implant it calls AVERAT in Taiwan. The targets it describes include mail-security appliances (SpamSniper) and telecom environments. Compromised Taiwanese devices, including NAS boxes, ADSL and fibre customer-premises equipment and Dahua DVRs, sat in a carrier’s address space: that means devices on a carrier’s network were compromised, not that the carrier itself was breached. AVERAT beacons over TCP port 25 every 600–699 seconds. It opens like a normal SMTP session, with EHLO and then STARTTLS, before switching to its own encryption, so it blends into mail traffic. Rapid7 names no actor. It says the activity is consistent with the China-nexus pattern of building networks out of compromised edge devices, “rather than confirmed membership” of any group. The detection cues it gives are processes running from deleted binaries, raw packet-filter sockets, and outbound port-25 connections from processes that are not mail servers.

_threatfeed.source_name: Rapid7
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 2 Oct 2026

items.title: Microsoft details Star Blizzard’s “RedFlick” phishing chain, which installs the CosmicPulse backdoor — at least 13 campaigns against more than 100 organisations, mostly in the US and UK
items.content_text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported on 29 September on Star Blizzard, which it describes, citing CISA’s attribution, as subordinate to Centre 18 of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Between January and August 2026 Microsoft saw at least 13 large-scale phishing campaigns affecting more than 100 organisations, mainly in the United States and the United Kingdom. The targets are Ukrainian people and institutions and the NGOs, think tanks and governments that support Ukraine policy, across diplomacy, finance, academia and security research. The technique Microsoft calls RedFlick starts with emails about password-protected archives; when a recipient replies, a follow-up brings a RAR or ZIP file with a malicious link. The chain then runs a shortcut file, a batch script and an MSI installer, sets scheduled tasks, and installs CosmicPulse, a Python backdoor that downloads and runs further payloads and executes remote commands. The reply step is the point: by the time anything malicious arrives, the target is in what looks like a real conversation.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Threat Intelligence
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaigns Jan–Aug 2026; published 29 Sep 2026

items.title: Proofpoint says the China-aligned group TA419 phished US AI-policy experts while posing as a former White House official, an economist and a senior Anthropic employee — the kit relays a real Microsoft sign-in and steals the session
items.content_text: Proofpoint reported on 1 October that TA419, which it calls “China-aligned and espionage-motivated”, ran credential-phishing campaigns from April 2025 to July 2026 against think tanks, universities, legal-sector organisations and policy institutes working on AI policy and national security in the United States and Japan. The lures impersonated a former deputy director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, an economist and a senior Anthropic employee, with themes such as an AI policy advisory committee, Senate reports on AI export controls and the military integration of Claude. Links passed through URL shorteners and a Cloudflare Turnstile check to a frameless browser-in-the-browser window that relayed the real Microsoft sign-in, adversary-in-the-middle style, capturing passwords, MFA codes and session cookies. Because the victim completes a genuine sign-in, ordinary MFA does not stop it. Proofpoint recommends phishing-resistant, origin-bound methods such as passkeys, and checking unexpected expert outreach through another channel.

_threatfeed.source_name: Proofpoint; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaigns Apr 2025–Jul 2026; published 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Microsoft’s Digital Defense Report 2026: the median time from a flaw’s discovery to its weaponisation is now well under a day, and government was the most-affected sector
items.content_text: Microsoft published its Digital Defense Report 2026 on 1 October, covering July 2025 to June 2026. Its headline for defenders is speed: the median time from discovery of a vulnerability to its weaponisation is now “well below 24 hours”, and Microsoft says AI-assisted post-compromise activity compresses work that used to take days into minutes. It names Chinese, Russian and North Korean state actors as using AI, and warns of a multi-year rise in known flaws left unpatched. In Microsoft’s chart of the sectors most affected by threat actors, government agencies and services account for 27%, IT 17%, research and academia 14% and communications infrastructure 9%. That chart counts all threat actors seen against Microsoft customers, not only state actors. The United States was the most affected country in January–June 2026, at 25.5%. It is one vendor’s view of its own telemetry, but the timing claim matches this edition: every KEV addition covered here came with a three-day federal deadline.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 1 Oct 2026

items.title: Cloudflare says its Containers service let one customer read another’s leftover data from reused storage blocks — fixed by 19 September, with no evidence the gap was used
items.content_text: Cloudflare disclosed on 27 September that its Containers product reused 64 KiB storage blocks without zeroing them, so a new container could read residual data left by another tenant. Its testing found residue on 18 of 24 placements, including SQLite databases, Chromium browser profiles and .env and credential files. The issue was reported on 4 September and fixed by 19 September, and Cloudflare says it found no evidence of data exposure through this method. This is a confirmed provider-side isolation flaw, now fixed, not an attack. For customers of any container or serverless platform, the useful question is what their workloads leave on disk.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cloudflare blog
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 4 Sep 2026; fixed by 19 Sep 2026; disclosed 27 Sep 2026

items.title: Two GitHub Actions compromised in May’s Mini Shai-Hulud campaign came back online in September with the credential stealer still inside — GitHub disabled them again on 25 September
items.content_text: Socket found that actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment, two GitHub Actions compromised in the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign of 18 May, became usable again in mid-September. Workflows that referenced them by version tag during that period ran the same obfuscated index.js payload, which takes tokens, credentials and CI/CD secrets from the runner. About 15,000 repositories depend on issues-helper. Not all of them will have run the payload in that period, and nobody has counted how many did. GitHub disabled both actions again on 25 September and has not explained how they were re-enabled without being cleaned. Reporting on the exact exposure window is imprecise; BleepingComputer describes activity from 16 September. The lesson is what “removed” means. A tag reference runs whatever the tag points to at the time, so a compromised action that is taken down and later restored comes straight back into every workflow that still names it.

_threatfeed.source_name: Socket; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Compromised 18 May 2026; re-enabled mid-Sep 2026; disabled again 25 Sep 2026

items.title: Microsoft profiles two ransomware operations: Storm-2570 moves between Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT with the same playbook, and Storm-3168 hit more than 100 Azure storage accounts in seven minutes from one leaked secret
items.content_text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published two reports on 24 and 25 September. Storm-2570, tracked since April 2025, is an affiliate that has deployed Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT ransomware against victims in the US, Canada, the UK, Spain, the Netherlands and Puerto Rico. Its targets span healthcare, education, government, financial services, energy, retail, IT, food and agriculture, NGOs, chemicals, critical manufacturing and transportation. The ransomware brand changes but the tradecraft does not: remote-management tools (Atera, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, Splashtop, NinjaRMM), PsExec, Impacket and NetExec to move laterally, Mimikatz, LaZagne and ntdsutil for credentials, and Rclone and s5cmd to exfiltrate. Microsoft says how it gets in “remains unconfirmed”. Storm-3168 is Microsoft’s name for the group Sysdig documented in July as JADEPUFFER and described as agentic ransomware. In one case from early June, an employee of the victim had posted an Azure service principal’s client ID, secret and tenant ID in plaintext in a public GitHub issue. After 15.5 hours of reconnaissance and more than 300 read operations, the attacker ran a seven-minute destructive sequence against more than 100 storage accounts, pulling storage keys more than 30 times and interfering with recovery. Microsoft’s warning: “Removing or redacting an exposed secret does not invalidate it.” That is one documented case, not a victim count, and neither report names victims.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Security Blog (two reports); Sysdig
_threatfeed.date_note: Storm-2570 report 24 Sep 2026; Storm-3168 report 25 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers turned MemTensor’s own GitHub Actions release workflows against it, took its npm and PyPI publish tokens, and shipped a self-spreading credential stealer
items.content_text: Aikido, SafeDep, Socket and StepSecurity reported on 23 September that attackers pushed commits that made MemTensor’s release workflows hand over its npm and PyPI publishing tokens. They then published malicious versions of @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin (0.1.21, 0.1.23 and 0.1.25) on npm and MemoryOS 2.0.34 on PyPI, which has since been quarantined. The payload, sckit, is a Go credential stealer for Windows, Linux and macOS. It takes .npmrc files, Vault tokens, SSH keys and AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, Slack, Stripe and SendGrid secrets, and uses any publishing rights it finds to push itself into more packages. The command-and-control domain is skyleen[.]fr. Download counts were not given, and the packages are niche tooling for AI-agent memory. The technique is what matters. The packages were published by the project’s own pipeline, so provenance checks would pass, the same weakness as the GHAPPIER case on this page. No attribution has been made.

_threatfeed.source_name: Aikido; SafeDep; Socket; StepSecurity; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Malicious releases and reports 23 Sep 2026

items.title: The first known malicious Terraform providers on the HashiCorp Registry deliver Go malware with blockchain and Slack command-and-control — researchers link them to North Korea’s fake-interview campaign
items.content_text: Aikido reported on 23 September two malicious Terraform providers on the HashiCorp Registry: kreuzwenker/docker, a typosquat of the widely used kreuzwerker/docker provider with 1,449 downloads, and gocommunity-io/dockerd with 222. It also found two Go modules, gocommunity.io/orderedbtree and gogets.dev/btreex. They deliver Go malware that uses the Ethereum Sepolia test network and Slack for command-and-control. The Hacker News describes this as the first known malicious payload delivery through the Terraform registry. The researchers link it to Graphalgo, a fake-recruiter campaign that ReversingLabs tied to North Korea in February. That link is researcher-assessed overlap, not an official attribution. HashiCorp had not commented in the reporting, and removal status was not stated. It is a different cluster from the TraderTraitor lock-file case on this page, but the target is the same: infrastructure engineers, whose laptops hold cloud credentials with production reach. A misspelt provider source in a .tf file is enough.

_threatfeed.source_name: Aikido; The Hacker News; ReversingLabs (Graphalgo background)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 23 Sep 2026

items.title: PHP2Shell: two critical PHP flaws leaked before patch day and drew millions of exploit attempts — PHP fixed them on 21 October, and no successful compromise has been confirmed yet
items.content_text: PHP released emergency updates on 21 October for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), memory-corruption flaws that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code through any PHP that serves web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed; PHP says mod_php is at highest risk. Details and both CVE IDs leaked about two days before the planned disclosure, and the UK NCSC told organisations to update or take PHP servers offline. Amazon says it saw a first exploitation attempt on 17 October, four days before the fixes; Cloudflare counted tens of thousands of attempts within 45 minutes of disclosure and millions by 22 October, some trying to install a Mirai-derived DDoS bot. As of 22–23 October no successful compromise had been confirmed, and the flaws are not in CISA KEV. On 23 October PHP disclosed a further flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that affects only an unusual session configuration and has no fix yet. Schneider Electric, ABB and Moxa have issued notices for products that embed PHP.

_threatfeed.source_name: PHP; Amazon and Cloudflare via BleepingComputer and The Hacker News; UK NCSC via BleepingComputer; CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01
_threatfeed.date_note: Leaked about 19 Oct 2026; attempts from 17 Oct; fixed 21 Oct 2026; CVE-2026-115560 disclosed 23 Oct 2026

items.title: Attackers chained Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to get root on fully patched VPNs — one link is still unpatched
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that attackers had chained three flaws in Connect Secure to run commands as root on appliances that were fully up to date, hitting what it calls a limited number of customers. Two of the flaws are fixed under one CVE, CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS 3.1 8.6), which CISA added to KEV the same day with a 16 October deadline. The third, a privilege escalation, has no CVE and no patch yet. Volexity found the chain during an incident response and tracks the actor as UTA0576, a group it had not seen before; exploitation dates to at least early October. The intruders planted no web shell, harvested domain credentials, LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, and wiped logs. Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may not spot it. As of 23 October no public CVE or fix for the third link had been found.

items.title: BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day CVE-2026-102764 is now in CISA KEV — a China-linked espionage group exploited it for about six weeks before a fix, and Mandiant warns of wider attempts
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline, which has now passed. BeyondTrust had published advisory BT26-05 on 15 October for the flaw (CVSS v4.0 9.3), improper validation of message origins in Remote Support’s internal messaging components that lets an attacker perform file operations on the appliance. The fix shipped on 8 October and BeyondTrust-hosted SaaS was patched on 9 October; BeyondTrust says it identified the defect on 28 September. Mandiant traced first exploitation to 29 August, against one BeyondTrust-hosted and one self-hosted appliance. The attackers, whom Mandiant and Google’s threat-intelligence team track as Armory Castle (also UNC5221 / Warp Panda) and BeyondTrust describes as state-sponsored espionage, used the Sawfly PHP web shell and the Bareclaw SOCKS5 tunneller, gained root, harvested credentials, deleted logs, moved laterally and took internal documents such as software inventories. Targets include SaaS providers, technology firms, government, legal services and business-process outsourcers, and Mandiant warns of possible widespread exploitation attempts. All Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 are affected. Remote-support tools hold standing access to the machines they support, which is why a single appliance matters.

items.title: Arista patches a third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months — CVE-2026-114625 lets any logged-in tenant user take operator control of an on-premises orchestrator
items.content_text: Arista disclosed on 22 October that CVE-2026-114625, an SQL injection in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), was detected by Arista and is known to be actively exploited. Any authenticated user, even one with the lowest built-in tenant role, can gain operator privileges and act as a local “superuser operator” on the system that pushes configuration to SD-WAN edges. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 (v4.0 9.4) and says the orchestrator is exposed by default, with no configuration that prevents it. Fixes are in 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; Arista-hosted and dedicated orchestrators are already patched, and gateways and edges are not affected. It follows CVE-2026-16812 in July and CVE-2026-93952 in September, so orchestrators patched last month need updating again. It was not in KEV as of CISA’s 21 October catalog, which predates the disclosure.

_threatfeed.source_name: Arista Security Advisory 0199; CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed and patched 22 Oct 2026; previous VCO zero-days Jul and Sep 2026

items.title: CISA’s KEV additions on 16 and 20 October: BeyondTrust, the FortiOS flaw behind the Peerstitch implant, Siemens Software Center abused in ClickFix attacks, four chained Plex flaws and a SiteGuard WAF bug
items.content_text: CISA added nine flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 and 20 October. On 16 October, both due 19 October: BeyondTrust Remote Support CVE-2026-102764 (see that card) and Fortinet CVE-2025-61624, a command-line path traversal in FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager, fixed in April, that Fortinet rates Medium and that needs privileged access. Unit 42 found it used to gain root on FortiGates managed by a telecom managed service provider and plant the Peerstitch implant, after initial access through FortiManager CVE-2024-47575; configuration and credential material for more than 500 managed firewalls was exposed, though Unit 42 has not confirmed intrusion into those networks. On 20 October: Siemens Software Center CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v3.1 6.7 / v4.0 8.4), which Siemens says the “Romulus” ClickFix campaign abuses by pairing its genuine signed binary with malicious DLLs, due 3 November; Plex Media Server CVE-2026-96652, -96654, -96655 and -96656, chained as “Plex2Shell” to drop cryptominers, due 23 October and 3 November; and SiteGuard Server Edition CVE-2026-106931, a command injection to root that its vendor confirms is being abused, due 23 October. No additions were found for 21–23 October.

items.title: GitLab’s second CVSS 10 flaw in ten days, CVE-2026-110264, could let an unauthenticated attacker run code on every self-managed release since 7.0 — instances patched for the previous one must upgrade again
items.content_text: GitLab released fixes on 21 October for CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS v3.1 10.0, GitLab), an integer overflow when the Onigmo regular-expression engine that GitLab ships compiles a crafted pattern, which under conditions GitLab has not described can let an unauthenticated user run code on the server. It affects Community and Enterprise Editions from 7.0 through 19.5.0 and is fixed in 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13; GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched, and there is no workaround. The same researcher reported CVE-2026-97229, the CVSS 10 CI/CD regular-expression flaw fixed on 13 October, so instances that moved to 19.4.2 or 19.3.5 for that fix still need 19.4.3 or 19.3.6. No exploitation is known and it is not in KEV; Shadowserver sees more than 2,700 exposed Community Edition instances. The 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 updates include database migrations that mean downtime on single-node installs.

_threatfeed.source_name: GitLab patch release; CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Shadowserver
_threatfeed.date_note: Fixed 21 Oct 2026; CVE published 22 Oct 2026; previous CVSS 10 fix 13 Oct 2026

items.title: Eight eMudhra certificate-authority keys turned out to be guessable — browsers have blocked them, Chrome drops an eMudhra root on 27 October, and eMudhra is leaving the TLS certificate business
items.content_text: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates, six for TLS and two for code signing, were generated with too little randomness at an April 2025 key ceremony, so they could be computed from the public certificates; one was reportedly the number four. Anyone holding them could have issued certificates trusted for any website or signed code that would be trusted. Chrome and Firefox blocked the intermediates on 17 October and Apple has also blocked them; Mozilla decided on 20 October to stop trusting the emSign ECC Root CA – G3, and Chrome stops trusting it on the morning of 27 October (Pacific). Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 hard-reject the keys (CVE-2026-111943), and Oracle’s 21 October Java SE and GraalVM alert CVE-2026-91403 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) is linked to the distrust by Red Hat. No misuse has been confirmed, and CERT-In says it has seen none. eMudhra revoked the certificates and is withdrawing from global TLS issuance; Chrome counted about 30,800 unexpired certificates under the root, almost all issued through InCommon, that must move to another CA.

_threatfeed.source_name: eMudhra via The Record; The Hacker News; Mozilla and Google root-programme decisions; CERT-In; CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported to root programmes 17 Oct 2026; Mozilla decision 20 Oct 2026; eMudhra exit 22 Oct 2026; Chrome distrust 27 Oct 2026

items.title: Oracle’s October Critical Patch Update carries 1,295 fixes and none is flagged as exploited — Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite and PeopleSoft lead, with several unauthenticated CVSS 9.8 flaws
items.content_text: Oracle released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update on 20 October with 1,295 new security patches; Tenable, quoted by SecurityWeek, counts 1,209 unique CVEs, 95 of them critical. The largest batches are Fusion Middleware (206, 134 of them remotely exploitable without authentication), E-Business Suite (194), Siebel CRM (122), Communications (110), PeopleSoft (109), JD Edwards (102), MySQL (98) and Java SE (55). Unauthenticated network flaws rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 include CVE-2026-75803 in Database Server (via OpenSSL), CVE-2026-91665 in Essbase and CVE-2026-101521 in APEX. Oracle flags none as exploited but repeats its warning that attackers go after flaws that are already patched, as ShinyHunters did with PeopleSoft this autumn (see that card). A separate 21 October Security Alert covers CVE-2026-91403 in Java SE and GraalVM (see the eMudhra card). The next quarterly update is due on 19 January 2027.
